requested.title: WebSocket route /ws/cron-log accepts unlimited anonymous connections with no rate limit, no cap, and no origin check
Unpinned module state splits the cron writer from the socket registry after a dev entry rebuild, silently breaking the demo
Route param `:id` collides with a sibling literal cache key, letting an unauthenticated GET poison the shared Pokémon-list cache for all visitors
Unbounded attacker-controlled cache keys on an unauthenticated, unrate-limited route grow a never-evicting in-memory Map and fan out to a third-party API
Redirect origin taken from the client-controlled Host header, bypassing the framework's `proxy.origin` pinning
Bare Bun route value silently opts `/demos/data-loading` out of the whole site middleware pipeline
`fail(400, { error })` from the form action is unreachable to the user — the page never reads a `form` prop
Session cookie set without the Secure attribute on an HTTPS production site
Unvalidated username length produces an oversized cookie and a false "signed in" state
Login form action has no rate limiting at any layer

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Every mechanical claim checks out: `/ws/cron-log` is mounted globally (site/src/routes.ts:395 spreads cronRoutes), it declares no `upgrade` handler so Mochi.ts:1293-1304 skips straight to `server.upgrade`, `checkRouteLimit` is invoked only in the page (Mochi.ts:981) and api (Mochi.ts:1211) branches, `Mochi.ws()` (Mochi.ts:227-232) genuinely accepts no `rateLimit`, KIND_POLICY sets `csrf: false` for ws (requestSetup.ts:66), `handle` middleware is never called in the ws branch, and the site's `protect()` only matches `/demos/protection*`. What does not hold is the impact. There is no amplification: each upgrade costs one `JSON.stringify` of at most 100 tiny rows (~6 KB) plus one socket write — strictly cheaper than an SSR page render on the same site, and `packages/site` sets no global `rateLimit`, so every page route is an equally unlimited and more expensive target. The registry is not unbounded in production: Mochi dispatches `close` through a live `wsHandlersMap.get(...)` lookup (Mochi.ts:2006) and `removeClient` deletes the entry, so the Set tracks only concurrent sockets and is bounded by the OS fd limit. The missing Origin check grants nothing here, because the socket carries no authentication and `message()` is a no-op `{}` — there is no cross-site WebSocket hijacking target, and a third-party page can already issue cross-origin `fetch`es to any endpoint on the host, so driving upgrades from visitors' browsers is not a new primitive. Finally, the repo's own prescribed pattern does not do what the finding says it should: the chat demo's `upgrade` derives a `rateKey` but rate-limits *messages*, not connections, and the framework exposes no ws-upgrade limiter at all — so this is a framework feature gap, not a defect this route introduced. Combined with the project's instruction to judge `packages/site/src/demos/*` as documentation, there is no concrete attack with material impact to describe.

I verified the whole chain end to end. `log` (cron.server.ts:7), `seq` (:8) and `clients` (:11) are plain module bindings. On a watched entry-graph edit, devWatcher's `buildEntry()` calls `extractServeOptions(outFile, { fresh: true })`, producing a brand-new `cron.server.ts` instance with an empty `log`, `seq = 0` and an empty `clients`. `applyRouteChanges` then hits the in-place ws branch and does `wsHandlersMap.set(pattern, handler.handlers)`, so all *new* sockets register into the new instance's Set. The decisive link is `reconcileCron`: `cronSignature` (cron.ts:78-80) hashes only `[name, schedule, tz, dev]` — not the handler — so a route-only edit leaves the signature identical and `reconcileCron` returns early without calling `startCronRuntime`. bun-boss therefore keeps the worker registered at boot, and `cronWorkHandler(job)` (queue.ts:898-904, wired at :983) closed over the *old* `job`, whose `run` references the old module's `log`/`seq`/`clients`. So the cron keeps appending to the orphaned `log` and broadcasting to the orphaned Set while every new socket is registered elsewhere: the page connects, reports connected, gets an empty snapshot from the new (empty) `log`, and never receives another row. The leak is real too — because `close` is dispatched via a live `wsHandlersMap.get(...)` lookup (Mochi.ts:2006), a pre-reload socket's close goes to the *new* `removeClient` and never clears the old Set, and the live bun-boss closure pins the old module instance so nothing is collected. The framework documents exactly this trap (170-development-mode.md:88, prescribing `pinGlobal`) and warns on it at runtime (`recompile:module-churn`, events.ts:473 / consoleLogger.ts:418), and the site already uses `pinGlobal` elsewhere (lib/docs.ts:55, lib/blog.ts:30, lib/highlight.server.ts:68). Dev-only, no production or security impact — BUG severity is correct.

The collision and the poisoning write are real and I confirmed every link. `params.id` is the raw Bun route param (`extractParams` reads `req.params`; Mochi.ts:1465 documents that params are URL-decoded), surfaced to the component through the `__mochiCtxProxy('params')` in mochi-env.server.js; `(params.id ?? 'pikachu').toLowerCase()` leaves `list:151` untouched, so `pokemon:${id}` is byte-identical to the sibling literal `pokemon:list:151`. Pages are slash-mirrored (KIND_POLICY `trailingSlash: true`), so `/demos/data-loading/list:151/` matches without a redirect. `MochiCache.run()` (cache.ts:348-352) coalesces strictly on `inflight.get(key)` and discards the caller's `fn`, and the ordering is deterministic rather than racy: `Promise.all`'s array literal invokes the detail `fetch` first, both calls traverse an identical await chain (`fetchWithStatus` → `lookup` → `read` → the synchronous `MemoryStorage.getItem`), and `run` is a *synchronous* function that publishes `inflight.set(key, promise)` before returning — so the detail loader always owns the run and the list loader always coalesces onto it. In the 20-of-24-hour stale window `lookup` (cache.ts:153-166) fires `void this.run(key, detailFn, generation)` as the background revalidation, the write guard at cache.ts:368 passes (generation unchanged), and `{value: null}` lands on the shared list key. So an unauthenticated GET does overwrite shared cross-user cache state, renewably. I am downgrading severity because the stated impact is wrong: Svelte 5.57's `ensure_array_like` (server/index.js:435-442) and the client `each` (dom/blocks/each.js:211) both coerce `null`/falsy collections to `[]`, so `{#each options as option (option.name)}` renders zero options rather than throwing — there is no boundary placeholder, no failed-snippet, and no hydration throw. The realised effect is an empty `<select>` on one demo page for up to 4 hours, plus a self-inflicted 500 for the attacker in the fresh window (`pokemon` is the list array, so `pokemon?.types.map` throws at page top level, and pages are not auto-wrapped). The payload is also pinned to `null`: making the write non-null would require an `id` that is simultaneously `list:151` and a valid pokeapi id. Genuine defect and a genuine cache-poisoning primitive, but with a cosmetic ceiling.

Confirmed in full. `/demos/data-loading/:id` passes no `rateLimit` to `Mochi.page` (which does accept one, Mochi.ts:207-220) and `packages/site/src/index.ts` sets no server-wide `rateLimit`, so `routeLimiters.get(pattern)` is null and `checkRouteLimit` returns `{}` immediately (Mochi.ts:862-865). `pokemonCache` (site/src/lib/cache.ts) passes only `minTimeToStale`/`maxTimeToLive`, so `MochiCache` falls back to `new MemoryStorage()` (cache.ts:110) with neither `maxAge` nor `purgeInterval` — whose own docstring (cache-storage.ts:88-91) says it 'holds everything forever'. `MochiCache` never deletes on the read path: past `maxTimeToLive`, `lookup` recomputes and `run` *overwrites* the key via `setItem`, it never evicts. `id` is unvalidated and unbounded, and every distinct value is a guaranteed miss that writes a new Map entry (a 404 stores `{value: null}`), so the backing Map grows monotonically with the attacker-chosen key space — only `generations` is reclaimed (cache.ts:305-321), not `store`. The memory-pressure escape hatch is as weak as described: `respondToPressure` (memoryPressure.ts:69-80) calls `sweep()` on `'warning'`, and `MemoryStorage.sweep()` returns `{removed: 0}` unconditionally when `maxAge` is undefined (cache-storage.ts:132-135); only `'critical'` clears, and a cgroup OOM kill commonly arrives with no userspace signal. The outbound half is real too — every unique id issues a live request to a free third-party API under the site's IP. The SSRF caveat is correctly dismissed: the host is hardcoded and `encodeURIComponent` escapes `/` and `%`, so no traversal to other pokeapi paths. Sibling demos already demonstrate the fix (`charts/routes.ts:30`, `queue/routes.ts:13`, `rate-limit/routes.ts:11`), so the omission is an inconsistency rather than a site-wide convention. MEDIUM is appropriate for unbounded attacker-keyed memory growth on an unauthenticated, unlimited route of a deployed site.

The mechanism is confirmed. A plain function is a legal `MochiRouteValue` (types.ts:104-108, 309), so `registerRoutePattern` matches none of its `isMochiPage/Api/Ws/Sse/File` branches, returns `null` at Mochi.ts:1511, and the caller assigns it verbatim at Mochi.ts:1537 — `buildRequestContext` never runs, so neither `buildPublicUrl()` nor the site's `proxy: { origin, … }` pin (index.ts:201) is applied. `req.url`'s authority under `Bun.serve` does come from the inbound `Host` header — Bun's own changelog records 'Fixed `Request.url` not showing the value from the `Host` header' (bun-v0.3.0) — and the repo's `proxy.ts` docstring says the same thing in different words. `Response.redirect` requires an absolute URL, so the `Location` carries whatever origin `new URL(path, req.url)` resolved. I am downgrading from MEDIUM because the 'open redirect' framing does not hold, as the finding itself concedes: a victim's browser always sends the correct `Host` on a click, so there is no link-phishing vector, and the cache-poisoning variant requires a front-end cache keyed on path only plus an nginx that forwards an arbitrary `Host` — neither is verifiable, since there is no proxy config in this repo at all. What *is* deterministic is narrower: `Mochi.serve()` is called with no `tls`, so behind a TLS-terminating proxy `req.url` is always `http://`, meaning every legitimate visitor to `/demos/data-loading` gets a scheme-downgraded `Location: http://…` plaintext hop (which, combined with F8's missing `Secure`, would carry the path-`/` demo session cookie in the clear) while every framework-managed route on the site emits the pinned `https://` origin. A real defect that the framework explicitly provides a mitigation for and this route bypasses, but the security impact is Host/scheme reflection rather than an exploitable open redirect.

Fully verified and distinct from F5 — the fixes are not interchangeable (emitting a root-relative `Location` from a bare Bun route value would resolve F5 and leave all of F6 intact), so I am not marking either as a duplicate. The bare function on L5 type-checks as a `MochiRouteValue` because `BunRouteValue` includes `(req, server) => Response` (types.ts:104-108, 309), `registerRoutePattern` falls through every `isMochi*` guard and returns `null` (Mochi.ts:1511), and the else branch assigns it directly: `bunRoutes[pattern] = handler as BunRouteValue` (Mochi.ts:1537). Since `buildRequestContext` is never invoked for this pattern, the request skips everything the page/api wrappers layer on: the `handle` sequence (invoked at Mochi.ts:991 for pages — so `compress()`, `immutableAssets`, `helloWorld`, `asciiDog`, `analytics()`, `encodeDebugBarPaths`, `noCache` and the demo handles from index.ts:174-185 never run, leaving the response with no `Cache-Control` and the hit invisible to Umami), the `mochiEvents.emit('request', …)` access log, `finalizeCookieHeaders`, and the CSRF/rate-limit/debug-bar policies in KIND_POLICY. The trailing-slash claim is right too: Mochi.ts:1538 pushes the pattern onto `slashMirrorPatterns`, so both `/demos/data-loading` and `/demos/data-loading/` are answered by the raw function with no 308 to the canonical form, and because the emitted target omits its own trailing slash under `trailingSlash: 'always'` the visitor pays a 302 → 308 double hop. Nothing warns at the call site. BUG severity is correct — this is an observability/caching/correctness defect, not an exploitable vulnerability.

Confirmed. On the non-enhanced path, `isFormFail(result)` sets `ctx.form = { ok: false, action, status, data }` and re-renders via `renderComponent(req, ctx, resolveOpts, result.status)` (Mochi.ts:1143-1153), and `renderComponent` injects it as `{ ...baseProps, form: formProp }` (Mochi.ts:924-925). `DataLoading.svelte` declares no `$props()` destructuring at all and never references `form` or `getRequestContext().form` — I read the whole file — so the payload is silently discarded and the visitor gets a 400 that re-renders the page unchanged with no error text. The non-enhanced path is the right one here: `PokemonSelector.svelte`'s form is a plain `<form method="POST">` with no `{@attach enhance(...)}`, unlike the login demo's. Reachability holds as well, and interestingly it is coupled to F3: once the list key is poisoned to `null` the `<select>` renders with zero `<option>` children (Svelte coerces the null collection to `[]`), the browser omits the `pokemon` field entirely on the `<noscript>` submit, `formData.get('pokemon')` is null, `String(null ?? '')` is `''`, and the `fail` branch fires. A hand-crafted same-origin POST reaches it unconditionally. Minor, but a genuine defect — and more so because `files.ts` publishes this file verbatim as reference material, so it teaches `fail()` without ever showing how the result is consumed. BUG severity is right.

The mechanical claim is verified. `cookies.set()` merges `{ ...this.defaults, ...options }` (cookies.ts:95-99); `cookieDefaults` is `applyFilter('cookie:defaults', {}, { options })` (Mochi.ts:494), the site registers only a `consoleLogger:line` filter (index.ts:245-247), so `defaults` is the empty object and the per-call options at routes.ts:25-30 omit `secure` — the emitted `Set-Cookie` carries no `Secure` attribute (cookies.test.ts:108-114 confirms a falsy `secure` produces no `Secure`). No `Strict-Transport-Security` header appears anywhere in the repo, and the repo's own docs prescribe the fix (162-extensions.md:23,157). SKILL.md:24 does point code generators at the `login` demo for 'Build a login form', and `files.ts` publishes `routes.ts` and `session.ts`, so the pattern propagates. I am downgrading from MEDIUM for two reasons. First, the exploitable impact on this deployment is nil: the password is the literal `hunter2` printed on the page itself, and the session authorises nothing beyond rendering a username, so a stolen cookie gets an attacker nothing they could not mint themselves in one POST. Second, the finding's supporting claim is factually wrong — the framework's own protection-clearance cookie does *not* share the omission; Mochi.ts:1790 explicitly sets `secure: url.protocol === 'https:'`. So what remains is a real and verified missing-flag defect in published reference material, correctly judged as a documentation-quality bug rather than a MEDIUM vulnerability.

Verified. `username` is `String(formData.get('username') ?? '').trim()` with only an emptiness check (routes.ts:16-20), it is JSON-stringified and base64url-encoded straight into the token (session.ts:19), and `<input name="username" …>` in EnhancedLoginForm.svelte:56 carries no `maxlength`, so the field is unbounded in both the browser and the handler. The arithmetic works out: a ~3000-char username yields a ~3030-byte JSON payload, ~4040 bytes of base64, plus the `.` and the 22-char truncated HMAC and the 20-byte cookie name — right at the ~4096-byte name+value ceiling browsers silently enforce, so a little over 3000 characters is reliably discarded. The action still returns `success({ username })`, and the hydrated island assigns `currentUser = result.data.username` (EnhancedLoginForm.svelte:24-27), so the UI renders 'Signed in as …' for a session that was never stored; the next navigation re-runs `serverProps`, finds no cookie, and shows the login form again. The secondary observations also hold — the site passes no `bun.maxRequestBodySize`, so Bun's large default applies and a multi-megabyte field drives several copies through `trim` → `JSON.stringify` → `Buffer.from` → `toString('base64url')` → cookie serialisation, and the resulting oversized `Set-Cookie` would be rejected upstream rather than surfacing a usable error. Low impact and demo code, but a genuine, verifiable logic flaw in a published login template, which is exactly what BUG severity is for.

The factual premises are all correct — `Mochi.page` does accept `rateLimit` (Mochi.ts:207-220), `/demos/login` passes none, `packages/site/src/index.ts` sets no server-wide `rateLimit`, so `routeLimiters.get(pattern)` is null and `checkRouteLimit` short-circuits (Mochi.ts:862-865) — but nothing is actually bypassed and there is no exploitable consequence. There is no credential to guess: the password is the literal `hunter2`, printed in the page description (Login.svelte:11) and again in the form hint (EnhancedLoginForm.svelte:68), and any username is accepted, so brute force is meaningless. The per-request work is one `createHmac('sha256')` over a short string plus a cookie serialisation — cheaper than the SSR render that serves the page — so it is not a resource-exhaustion vector either, and the session it mints authorises nothing. Crucially, the absence of a limit is not specific to this route: the site configures no global `rateLimit`, so essentially every one of its ~100 routes is equally unlimited, and this login page is neither the most expensive nor the most sensitive among them. The only argument left is template propagation via SKILL.md:24, which is a documentation-polish suggestion rather than a vulnerability — and the project's guidance explicitly says to judge `packages/site/src/demos/*` (naming hardcoded `hunter2` and absent auth) as documentation, not product. The finding's own stated confidence is 'low' and it concedes it is not a credential-guessing risk; I agree, and there is no other impact to substitute.
